responseSet.title: Two Studies in Problems of Containment
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Two Studies in Problems of Containment

Kate Paul and Ann Zadik

Ann Zadik

Ann Zadik  

Introduction

While in training we each wrote a clinical paper. We subsequently realised that both papers seemed to show some of the same aspects of the problems of containment. The following introduction is an attempt to elucidate some of these problems.

Both the patients we describe manifest their anxieties first and foremost in physical and in concrete ways. Their behaviour illustrates the link between infantile phantasies about containment in body terms and the structure or lack of it in the mental functioning.

The mother, through physical and emotional caring, serves as a container for the infant's experiences. She gives them shape and space, making them more tolerable so that the infant may take them back into himself.

Insofar as either the infant is unable to tolerate frustration or the mother is unable to be a “good-enough” container, projective and introjective processes may be impaired.

The material to follow will show how the patients’ feelings colour external reality to such an extent that at times little differentiation is possible, hence little thought. The ensuing confusion shows itself in treatment through the transference, permeating all areas of the personality. The transference relationship expresses the confusion between the infant and parents; between inside and outside; between parts of the self; between body and mind; between good and bad. The patients live in a world peopled largely by the products of their own mind, and symbolization cannot develop.

In the therapeutic process, the room, the session times, the boundaries and limits set by the therapists are attacked in various ways. A healthy link with their objects, carrying with it the implication of separateness, is experienced by the patients as extremely threatening. On the one hand, persecution or the inadequacy of a damaged object is feared; on the other hand, in moments of greater confidence, there may be an inability to allow their object a life of its own.

The therapist experiences these concrete anxieties and in giving them a voice and a context gives them a container. Experiences and anxieties may become tolerable and hence available for consideration. This derives from the to-and-fro and the containment in the relationship between the mother and infant. When the child can internalize the mother or the therapist as a container, then he can experience the relief from frustration that understanding can give.

responseSet.title: William McGuire editor. The Freud/Jung letters: The correspondence between Sigmund Freud and CG. Jung. Hogarth Press/Routledge and Kegan Paul, London, 1974, £7.95.
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

William McGuire editor. The Freud/Jung letters:The correspondence between Sigmund Freud and CG. Jung. Hogarth Press/Routledge and Kegan Paul, London, 1974, £7.95.

Barbara Forryan

Barbara Forryan

Barbara Forryan  

The members of both Freud's and Jung's family wished these letters to be published as historical documents, and this they undeniably are. The story of their preservation and pathway to publication is itself a fascinating one.

Many readers will hope to learn more from these letters of the causes of the rift between these two great minds. The great attraction they had for each other is movingly evident in the early letters, where Freud writes to Jung with a warmth and love that is missing even in his letters to Abraham.

Jung always wrote that Freud's narrow view of sexuality as the basis of mental disorder was unacceptable to him, and his doubts on its applicability to dementia praecox (schizophrenia) are documented in his letters from 1907 onwards. However, other analysts including Abraham were able to develop their insight into the psychoses within the framework of Freud's theory, and to modify or extend his theory without breaking away from the psychoanalytic movement. Jung's letters in 1907 asked for Freud's help in his analysis of schizophrenic patients in the Burgholzli mental hospital; different readers will find different clues in the letters as to why Freud could not give the right help or why Jung could not use it. Some of Freud's key replies are missing; from the context they seem to be letters containing criticisms of Jung's writing.

The loss that Jung represented to psychoanalysis can be measured already in these early years; his remarks on children's dreams, on the analytic material from his own little daughter, and on Freud's Interpretation of Dreams, axe perceptive and far-reaching.

Earlier readers of the unpublished letters were reported as being disappointed with their trivial contents: it is true that from 1908 the letters no longer contain much exchange of ideas (unlike Freud's correspondence with Lou Andreas-Salome) but a statement on one side met by silence on the other. The “going-wrong” of the relationship seems never to have been openly discussed; the letter Jung's wife wrote to Freud about this is movingly, strikingly different from the rest of the book.

responseSet.title: Child Psychotherapy at the Institute of Child Psychology
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Child Psychotherapy at the Institute of Child Psychology

John Hood-Williams MA DIPICP

John Hood-Williams

John Hood-Williams  

In this article an attempt will be made to give an account of the way the psychotherapy of children is conducted at the Institute of Child Psychology, and to outline the main principles developed by its founder, the late Dr Margaret Lowenfeld, which have determined the rationale of this mode of child psychotherapy.

Historical Background

To do this, it is necessary first to say something about how Dr Lowenfeld arrived at the views she held and taught.

With a background of children's medicine that had alerted her to the importance of emotional factors in children's illnesses, and with wide reading in psychology and psychoanalytic theory, in 1928 she set up the Children's Centre, which developed in 1933 into the Institute of Child Psychology.

Into the two rooms of the Children's Centre she brought children referred to her from widely differing social backgrounds and suffering from a wide variety of difficulties in physical, emotional or intellectual functioning. Play equipment was at first minimal, and was added to as children indicated their needs.

The children were allowed to make whatever use of the material they chose, and to combine together in groups or not as they chose. There were only a few common-sense rules about damage and injury, otherwise they were free to do as they wished. Dr Lowenfeld and her co-workers tried to minimise the fact that they were adults vis-a-vis the children, and tried to maintain a friendly but non-involved attitude towards them.

As far as it is possible to do so, they tried to have no preconceptions about what behaviours they expected of the children nor of what they hoped would emerge from the study.

Extremely detailed records were kept of what happened during the children's attendances at the Centre, as the object of the study was to see what does actually happen when children are given the chance to play freely with minimal adult involvement or interference and a plenitude of material with which to realise their play intentions.

Nothing quite like this had ever been done before, and the results were surprising. For one thing, many of the children got better. Enuretics ceased wetting their beds, disruptive and unruly children became calmer, asthmatics became symptom-free, children failing at school for lack of concentration became able to concentrate and succeeded at school, withdrawn children became outgoing.

responseSet.title: The First Year of the Analysis of A Boy Showing Neurotic and Atypical Features
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The First Year of the Analysis of A Boy Showing Neurotic and Atypical Features

Marlene Robinson

Marlene Robinson

Marlene Robinson  

This case deals with an eight year old child who came into treatment presenting a complex and double sided picture. On the one hand, Tim seemed to be suffering from neurotic conflicts which manifested themselves in the forms of eating difficulties and sleep disturbances. This would imply that he had a relatively strong ego, which, when confronted with conflict at various stages of development, forced symptom formation.

… Symptoms are created in order to remove the ego from a situation of danger. If the symptoms are prevented from being formed the danger does in fact materialize; that is … the ego is helpless in the form of a constantly increasing instinctual demand

(Freud S. 1926)

However, coupled with this was the problem of his intense aggressive outbursts (directed towards himself and others), which he was unable to control, plus his conscious, horror-filled and violent phantasy life (shown quite clearly in his initial psychiatric and psychological test interviews). This would indicate that his ego was weak, and unable to deal with his overwhelming impulses which were experienced as a continuous threat.

It became apparent very early in treatment that the technical handling of a child with such dual presenting pictures would be on two levels.

Treatment firstly entailed “ego-building”, or ego support, whereby the therapist helped to control overwhelming drives when the child could not. By siding with the child's weak ego, and by helping to contain explosive impulses, the therapist was experienced as a safe, protective object. The external object helped to reinforce the child's inadequate internal structure.

A great deal of Tim's first year of treatment was on this level, as it was essential that a trust with the therapist be established before acknowledgement and interpretations of his violent phantasy world could be made. When these were touched upon too early, Tim reacted with great anxiety, and he needed to protect himself from the dangerous therapist whom he felt as part of his threatening underworld. Therefore, the verbalisation of his anxiety, and not interpretations of wishes behind his aggressive phantasies and behaviour, which would merely have increased his panic, was necessary for providing a safe background against which the second level of treatment—analysis of conflicts—could take place. When this occurred, the healthier side of the child was reached, and gave a more optimistic outlook on the case.

responseSet.title: The Development of Containment in a Three to Five Year Old Boy
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Development of Containment in a Three to Five Year Old Boy

Kate Paul

Kate Paul

Kate Paul  

When Malcolm J started five times weekly psychoanalytic psychotherapy he was three years old. Two years later treatment was continuing and was likely to be needed for some time to come. Using material from these first two years, I describe how anxieties about separation and containment arose in the treatment.

Firstly I outline the referral and history. I then go on to describe the first few chaotic months of treatment. Malcolm at first attempts to invade and control the therapist using the most concrete means at his disposal: his own excreta and physical attacks. He lives in a state of ceaseless anxiety with several weeks of constant diarrhoea and some hallucinations in the sessions. Then as he gradually becomes aware of the containment provided in the treatment, he begins to symbolise his anxieties more and to keep some of his most extreme feelings in the therapy room and in the transference. He becomes able to attend playgroup, of which he had previously been too frightened. Treatment is now established.

The following year is briefly outlined, with particular reference to the theme of containment.

Finally I give an account of several months in the second year. Malcolm fabricates and talks about a series of containing vehicles for himself; he uses these as alternatives to what he feels to be the hazards of maintaining contact with the therapist as a container. These airborn vehicles move gradually earthwards as Malcolm comes closer to direct emotional contact and to standing on his own feet, outside his object. The secondary containers then recede into the background as Malcolm begins to explore his relationship with the therapist as a primary container. The move earthwards is connected to a number of other changes. Perhaps the most important of these is an increased trust in peoples’ ability to survive his attacks and respond to and contain his feelings. This entails Malcolm beginning to accept the therapist in the transference as a mother fruitfully linked to a father and children.

responseSet.title: The First Year of Treatment of an Adolescent Girl: Attempts at Containment
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The First Year of Treatment of an Adolescent Girl: Attempts at Containment

Ann Zadik

Ann Zadik

Ann Zadik  

Mary was seventeen years old and a student at a technical college doing a secretarial training course. When I had my first contact with her she was at school, and soon to take her O-level exams.

She has two sisters, both quite a lot older than she is. The elder is married and living away from home, the other is still at home.

Mary lives with her parents and this one sister in a Council flat. Her father, whom she described in strong terms as an isolated, bad-tempered and bitter man, works the night-shift and sleeps by day. Her mother works as a cleaner by day, and so, it seems, things are arranged so that there is a bare minimum of contact between her parents. Her mother reported that her pregnancy with Mary was unplanned and unwanted, as it put severe financial strain on the family.

I would like to begin by describing how Mary came to the Clinic, as I think it gives a good composite picture of some of the characteristics of this girl, her position as she perceives it, and the feelings she evokes. There is a sense of bravado, something slightly audacious about her, but also her courage comes through.

She had been going to her G.P. for some time with the complaint of urinary frequency. She had been given some medication but, she said, it did not help, and eventually she requested her G.P. to send her somewhere where she could talk about what she has steadfastly referred to as her “loo problem”. She described her problem as having to go to the toilet much more than a normal person and having to go very suddenly.

I began seeing her five times a week. I would like to describe what happened between us in the first year of treatment. I say “happened” because the nature of the first year's interchange was not one which allows any large general statement to be formulated.

The material shows the primitive level of her functioning. She communicated with great intensity, not so much through words, as through actions, through doing (which, not incidentally, provoked enormous worry in me). What we were primarily arriving at was Mary's awareness that things happened, but not why, and then how Mary felt that things had altered, that they had changed, again in a very concrete and basic way.

responseSet.title: Doubly Deprived
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Doubly Deprived**

Gianna Henry

Gianna Henry

Gianna Henry  

I intend to present some aspects of my work with a patient whom I have been treating for just over two years, initially on a once weekly basis and twice a week since June 1973. Martin was referred to the Clinic for very considerable learning difficulties, (he was nearly fourteen when he started treatment and his reading age was six), for aggressive behaviour and stealing. He had made a suicidal attempt two years prior to referral when he tried to jump from a second floor window.

History

Martin is the illegitimate child of West Indian parents. His mother died when he was seven years old, but she had had no contact with Martin after he had been placed in residential care; he was at the time two months old. His father had disappeared at the beginning of the mother's pregnancy. Martin had three placements up to the age of two, when he was fostered by an English couple with a child of their own, a boy four years older than Martin. He was with the foster parents for ten years until fostering broke down. Martin was at the time twelve years old. It seems that the foster parents found Martin increasingly unmanageable because of his stealing and very defiant behaviour. They had reached the point where they felt that they were “unable to accept him or have any trust in him”. There is no indication of the impact that the attempted suicide one year before the breakdown of fostering, might have had on the foster parents and how it might possibly have contributed to their feeling at a loss. They reported that the difficulties with Martin had very considerably increased from the time when he was informed of his natural mother's death. He was then seven years old.

When Martin left the foster home, he returned to a Children's Home and apparently there were no outward signs of his being distressed about the move. There are many indications in the case history of the foster parents’ deep feeling of failure in their relationship with Martin, and they saw his coldness and detachment as confirmation that they had never meant a greal deal to him. The first contact after the move to the Children's Home was a phone call which had to be cut short because the foster mother was crying so much she could not talk. Both foster parents had visited Martin at the Home. Their son refused to come because he said “Martin had hurt his mother too much”. They left after meeting Martin feeling that “nothing had happened. He appeared to have happily settled himself down”. They said they would prefer to discontinue contact with Martin and have in fact completely lost touch with him since then.

responseSet.title: Us and Them? - The Child, The Analyst and the Parents
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Us and Them? - The Child, The Analyst and the Parents

John Bolland MB CHB, MRCPSYCH

John Bolland

John Bolland  

It is deeply regretted that Dr. John Bolland died suddenly in April 1974. A few weeks before his death he gave a talk, based upon a version of this paper, to a meeting of the Association of Child Psychotherapists. His paper stimulated a thoughtful and vigorous discussion and Dr. Bolland agreed to its publication in this Journal. He died before being able to complete the further work on the paper which he had planned to undertake. This posthumous paper is now published by kind permission of his wife, Jill Bolland.

Editor's Note

Counter-transference in child analysis is not often discussed in the literature. In a paper entitled “Techniques of child analysis: problems of counter-transference” published in the International Journal of Psychoanalysis in 1971, Kohrman, Fineberg, Gelman and Weiss reproached child analysts for their neglect of the topic. They complained further that such counter-transference problems are treated in the literature with a discretion which is perhaps over-delicate. As a child analyst my reactions to their paper were somewhat mixed. I felt that I was being scolded for not doing my homework, and that they were not making sufficient allowance for the painfulness of some aspects of counter-transference and the consequent reluctance to publish studies of it. Nevertheless, there is much substance in their assessment of the situation, and I particularly liked the discussion of how knowledge of counter-transference phenomena might be used to further the course of an analysis.

I have been used for some years now to talking with some social worker, psychology and child psychotherapy colleagues about all kinds of feelings concerning children and their parents in connection with my work at the Child Guidance Training Centre. Our therapeutic work there takes the form of once-weekly psychotherapy and is based on the premise that children do not exist in a vacuum, that a child is not just a neat little parcel consisting of an unconscious plus an assortment of defence mechanisms, that the environment surrounds, enfolds, invades the child and that he also affects the environment—there is interaction at all levels between the child and others. When the child comes into treatment another interaction is added, and because of my psychoanalytic training I use the transference as the main means of trying to understand what goes on in the child I am treating. I would be sadly neglecting the possibilities inherent in the treatment interaction if I ignored my contribution to it. In my experience discussion of counter-reactions is much more free in connection with psychotherapy than it is with psycho-analysis. This seems even more off when you think of the considerable amount of thought given to, and published, about the same problems in the analysis of adults. Could it be that counter-transference in relation to children is not quite respectable among child analysts?
